TSSA pressure vessel inspection in Ontario: periodic inspection requirements for owners

Direct answer: In Ontario you may not operate a regulated boiler or pressure vessel without a current TSSA Certificate of Inspection (O. Reg. 220/01, section 5). To keep that certificate you need a periodic inspection within the maximum interval set in TSSA's Code Adoption Document. For a general pressure vessel that is no more than three years. TSSA inspects uninsured equipment, and the boiler and machinery insurer, or a third-party provider it retains, inspects insured equipment.

The section above is aimed at companies seeking TSSA authorisation. This section covers the owner and operator side: what a periodic inspection is, how often it is due, who may perform it, how the Record of Inspection and Certificate of Inspection cycle works, and how repairs, NDE and an API 510 programme fit around it. It is based on TSSA's published pages and its Code Adoption Document Amendment BPV-25-01 Revision 1 (published 15 May 2026, effective 15 June 2026), which replaced earlier amendments and adopts CSA B51-24. Some older guidance, including parts of this page, cites BPV-20-01 or B51-19. Check the current amendment on tssa.org before relying on any clause.

Maximum periodic inspection intervals in Ontario

Direct answer: Table 1 of the current Code Adoption Document sets maximum intervals by equipment type: deaerators 1 year, high-pressure boilers 1 year, low-pressure boilers 2 years, pressure vessels 3 years, pressure vessels with quick-opening doors 1 year, and electrochemical cell stacks (ECS) for hydrogen electrolysis 1 year. Hydropneumatic and cushion tanks now fall under the general 3-year pressure vessel interval.

Equipment (CAD Table 1)Maximum periodic inspection intervalPractical note
Deaerator1 yearDeaerators are prone to cracking at welds, so owners often add wet fluorescent MT to the annual inspection
High-pressure boiler1 yearIncludes its fittings. Relief device servicing evidence is checked at the inspection
Low-pressure boiler2 yearsCommon in commercial and institutional buildings
Pressure vessel3 yearsCovers most process vessels, receivers, separators and drums, and now hydropneumatic and cushion tanks
Pressure vessel with a quick-opening door1 yearAutoclaves, sterilisers and filter housings. The closure interlock is a focus
Electrochemical cell stack (ECS)1 yearOntario treats hydrogen electrolysis stacks as pressure vessels throughout their life cycle

These intervals are maximums. The inspector may direct an internal or external inspection, or a test of safety devices, as part of any periodic inspection. A Certificate of Inspection is valid for between 12 and 36 months depending on the interval. TSSA's own example is that a device inspected every 24 months receives a certificate valid for 24 months. The CAD also says plainly that engineering assessments do not override TSSA's minimum periodic inspection cycle. So whatever an API 510 calculation or a risk-based study suggests, the jurisdictional inspection must still happen on time.

Some classes are exempt from periodic inspection under section 5.1 of the CAD. They include refrigerant pressure vessels and receivers (unless the refrigerant is ammonia), blowdown tanks, water-to-water heat exchangers, and small compressed-air receivers within stated pressure and volume limits. Certificates for exempt items do not need renewal. Items below the regulation's size thresholds, such as standalone fittings not attached to regulated equipment, fall outside O. Reg. 220/01 entirely. If you are unsure whether an item is exempt, ask TSSA. Do not assume.

Who may perform the periodic inspection

Direct answer: Uninsured equipment is inspected by a TSSA inspector. Insured equipment is inspected by the boiler and machinery insurer, which may hire a third-party inspection provider that holds a TSSA certificate of authorization. In every case the person inspecting must hold a valid Ontario Certificate of Competency.

The Code Adoption Document sets out each route in detail:

  • Ontario Certificate of Competency. Applicants must pass TSSA's own Certificate of Competency examination and the National Board In-service Commission examination. They must also meet the National Board's education and experience credit rules (NB-263, RCI-1) or qualify under the NB-380 programme. To apply, renew or reinstate, they need a valid National Board In-service Commission or another certification the Director accepts, and they must keep up continuing education.
  • Insurers. An insurer that underwrites regulated equipment is responsible for its periodic inspection. TSSA audits or surveys active insurers, normally every three years, for compliance with the regulation and the CAD.
  • Third-party inspection providers. A provider working for an insurer needs a TSSA certificate of authorization. The application includes National Board accreditation as an Authorized Inspection Agency or an equivalent certificate TSSA accepts, the list of Certificate of Competency holders, and a quality control manual. Authorizations are renewed every three years.
  • Owners. An owner's own API 510 inspector does not, by that certification alone, perform the jurisdictional periodic inspection. Owner-user self-inspection is a separate TSSA authorization. For repairs, it is the Owner/User Self-Inspection Repair Program.

An NDE company is not on that list, and that includes Atlantis. NDE technicians produce data that the Certificate of Competency holder uses. They do not perform or sign the periodic inspection.

The Certificate of Inspection cycle, step by step

Direct answer: Request the inspection well before the certificate expires. TSSA suggests scheduling insured inspections about 60 days ahead. The inspector issues a Record of Inspection to you and to TSSA within 30 days. You then have 30 days from receiving it to validate the record and pay on TSSA's BPV portal, after which TSSA issues the renewed certificate.

  1. Schedule. Contact your insurer, or TSSA for uninsured equipment, ahead of the expiry date. TSSA warns owners to allow enough time to meet the 30-day Record of Inspection deadline, because renewal, including payment, has to be completed before the existing certificate expires.
  2. Prepare the equipment. Arrange isolation, entry permits, cleaning and insulation removal where the inspector will need internal or close external access. Also gather the documents listed in the checklist below.
  3. Inspection. The inspector does the internal and external inspection and any tests they direct. They review relief device servicing evidence against the CSA B51 and B52 servicing requirements adopted by the CAD.
  4. Record of Inspection (ROI). Within 30 days the inspector issues an ROI for each item. It records the TSSA unique identifier, owner and site details, inspection date, inspection type (internal or external), the inspector's Certificate of Competency number, inspection status, MAWP, CRN and any reportable violations. When TSSA itself inspects, its inspection report serves as the ROI.
  5. Validate and pay. Check the ROI on the BPV portal, correct any errors through the inspector, and pay within 30 days. If your ROI does not appear, contact the insurer or provider.
  6. Certificate issued. TSSA issues the Certificate of Inspection, which you can download from the portal.

Violations. TSSA Director's Order BPV-25-02 sorts 20 reportable violations into two groups: high-risk and other. A high-risk violation must be fixed immediately, and no certificate is issued until an ROI showing the fix has been submitted. Other reportable violations must be fixed within the time the insurer or provider sets.

Notifications and records. Owners must notify TSSA in writing within 10 calendar days when equipment is removed from service, when the owner, operator or insurer changes, or when a defect is found that makes the equipment unsafe to operate (in that case, tell the insurer as well). Owners and insurers must keep inspection reports for six years from the inspection date.

What the periodic inspection involves, and where NDE fits

Direct answer: The jurisdictional inspection is the Certificate of Competency holder's examination of the vessel, its fittings and its safety devices, internal and external as they direct. NDE comes in when visual inspection is not enough. Typical cases are thickness where corrosion is active, cracking in susceptible services, and areas the inspector cannot see.

A visual internal and external inspection is enough for many small vessels. Larger process vessels, and those in corrosive or cracking services, usually need examinations that only NDE can provide:

  • Ultrasonic thickness at CMLs to confirm the vessel is still above the thickness its MAWP requires, and to support corrosion-rate trending. See UT thickness monitoring.
  • Corrosion mapping where corrosion is localised, such as the bottoms of separators and drums, under deposits, or at liquid-level lines. See corrosion mapping.
  • Wet fluorescent MT, PT or phased array for cracking in deaerators, amine, caustic and wet H2S services, and at weld toes on cyclic equipment. See phased array inspection.
  • External screening for corrosion under insulation on insulated vessels before the inspector decides how much insulation to strip. See CUI inspection.
  • Radiography where a volumetric weld record is needed. In Ontario, as in all provinces, exposure devices and their operators are licensed federally by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission. See CNSC requirements.

Doing the NDE before the inspector's visit, during the same outage, often saves an extra shutdown. The inspector can then review the readings, ask for follow-up where needed, and complete the inspection without a second mobilisation. The report should identify each vessel by its TSSA unique identifier and CRN as well as the owner's tag, so it matches the ROI.

Where API 510 fits in an Ontario programme

Direct answer: TSSA's current Code Adoption Document does not list API 510 or API 570 among its adopted references. Ontario refineries and chemical plants still run API 510 programmes as their engineering practice. The TSSA periodic inspection sets the legal minimum. API 510 adds corrosion-based intervals, CML trending and remaining-life discipline inside that minimum.

The practical consequence is a two-calendar plan. Every vessel gets an API 510 due date from its inspection plan and a TSSA due date from its Certificate of Inspection, and work is booked to whichever comes first. A general process vessel's TSSA cycle is three years at most, so a vessel with a long API 510 internal interval may still need a jurisdictional inspection in between. Well-planned on-stream NDE can support that inspection without opening the vessel, if the Certificate of Competency holder accepts it. For the API 510 side, see the API 510 code explained. For how other provinces handle API 510, see API 510, 570 and 653 in Canada.

Repairs, alterations and hot taps under TSSA

Direct answer: In Ontario, repairs and alterations to a pressure-retaining component need TSSA's prior agreement. Alteration designs go to TSSA for review and approval. The NBIC Part 3 is the guide for repair and alteration procedures, but TSSA does not accept the NBIC "routine repair" category, so every such job is treated as a repair. Hot taps need TSSA acceptance of the procedure before work starts.

  • Organisations doing repairs and alterations need a TSSA certificate of authorization for that scope. An owner who wants to inspect its own repairs needs TSSA's Owner/User Self-Inspection Repair Program authorization.
  • Replacement material with a different P-number from the original design is treated as an alteration.
  • Where the NBIC and CSA B51 disagree, Ontario's CAD says B51 prevails.
  • NDE on repairs is done to the procedures and acceptance criteria of the construction code and the repair plan. Keep the reports with the repair record, because the next periodic inspector will ask for them.

NDE personnel certification in Ontario

Direct answer: CSA B51 points NDE personnel to CAN/CGSB-48.9712 (ISO 9712) or another acceptable standard. Ontario's CAD amends that clause to say that ASNT SNT-TC-1A is also acceptable. The owner's specification and the inspector can still require a particular scheme for a particular job.

The Canadian General Standards Board closed on 1 April 2026. Natural Resources Canada's NDT Certification Body continues to certify personnel to CAN/CGSB-48.9712, and the standard itself is being maintained within NRCan. Specifications written before 2026 that say "CGSB certified" should be read, and preferably rewritten, as "certified by NRCan's NDTCB to CAN/CGSB-48.9712". See NRCan NDT certification. Atlantis technicians are certified to ASNT SNT-TC-1A under Level III oversight, which Ontario's adoption expressly accepts. If your specification calls for CAN/CGSB-48.9712 on a given method, tell us at scoping.

Owner checklist before a TSSA periodic inspection

  • Current Certificate of Inspection, expiry date and TSSA unique identifier for each item.
  • CRN and manufacturer's data report. For older equipment, confirm design registration is on file.
  • Previous Records of Inspection and any open violations, with evidence they have been fixed.
  • Relief device servicing records for every primary overpressure protection device.
  • Repair and alteration records since the last inspection, with TSSA agreements and NDE reports.
  • Your API 510 inspection plan, CML maps and latest thickness data for process vessels.
  • Isolation, entry and access arrangements, and an NDE scope agreed with the inspector in advance.
  • Your insurer's contact details and a booking made early enough to meet the 30-day ROI deadline.

TSSA periodic inspection: frequently asked questions

How often must a pressure vessel be inspected in Ontario?

At a maximum interval of three years for a general pressure vessel under the current Code Adoption Document. Vessels with quick-opening doors, deaerators and high-pressure boilers are on a one-year cycle, and low-pressure boilers on two years.

Who does TSSA boiler and pressure vessel inspections?

TSSA inspects uninsured equipment. For insured equipment the insurer is responsible, directly or through a TSSA-authorized third-party provider. The person inspecting must hold an Ontario Certificate of Competency.

What is a TSSA Certificate of Inspection?

It is the document that allows a regulated boiler or pressure vessel to operate in Ontario. It is valid for 12 to 36 months depending on the equipment's interval, and it is renewed after each periodic inspection through TSSA's BPV portal.

What happens if my Certificate of Inspection expires?

Operating without a current certificate is an offence under O. Reg. 220/01. Renewal, including payment, must be completed before expiry, so book the inspection early enough for the 30-day ROI process.

Which pressure vessels are exempt from TSSA periodic inspection?

Section 5.1 of the CAD exempts certain non-ammonia refrigerant vessels, blowdown tanks, water-to-water heat exchangers and small compressed-air receivers within stated limits. Check the current CAD or ask TSSA before treating an item as exempt.

Is API 510 required by TSSA?

TSSA's current CAD does not adopt API 510 or API 570 by reference. Many Ontario sites use API 510 as their engineering practice, but it does not replace or extend the TSSA periodic inspection cycle.

Can our NDE contractor perform the TSSA inspection?

No. NDE technicians supply examination data. The periodic inspection is performed and signed by a Certificate of Competency holder working for TSSA, the insurer or an authorized provider.

How long must inspection reports be kept in Ontario?

Owners and insurers must keep inspection reports for six years from the inspection date. Ask us to scope NDE for your next TSSA cycle.
